newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TENNIS-HINGIS STORMS INTO HISTORY AT AUSTRALIAN OPEN.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-HINGIS STORMS INTO HISTORY AT AUSTRALIAN OPEN.

text.p: Swiss teenager Martina Hingis became the youngest Grand Slam champion in modern tennis history on Saturday, storming past France's Mary Pierce in the final of the Australian Open.
The 16-year-old prodigy took only 59 minutes to seal a 6-2 6-2 victory with a near-perfect display of precision tennis which left former champion Pierce floundering.
"Martina played just a great match. She was too good for me today," Pierce told the crowd at the presentation ceremony. "I'm sure we will be seeing much more of her."

At 16 years, three months and 26 days, Hingis becomes the youngest singles champion at a major championship since amateur Lottie Dod won Wimbledon at 15 years and 10 months in 1887 -- before Grand Slams were invented.
Hingis had already claimed the honour of youngest Grand Slam champion by winning the women's doubles at Wimbledon last year.

The Czechoslovak-born world number four started the match as hot favourite after cruising through the woman's draw in Melbourne. The only question had been whether she might be hit by nerves in her first Grand Slam singles final.
But she saved three break points in the first game and never really looked back, taming Pierce's powerful groundstrokes with pinpoint passes and some delicate drop shots.

The unseeded Pierce took 20 minutes to get onto the scoreboard, holding her third service game and then breaking Hingis's serve to trail 2-5. Hingis broke her back in the next game to take the first set.
Pierce put up more opposition in the second set, but the outcome was never in doubt -- like a true champion, Hingis was able to step up her game at will.
Hingis broke Pierce at 3-2 in the second set and then again at 5-2, converting the first of three match points with a fierce forehand winner.
She was immediately congratulated by her mother and coach, Melanie, a former Czechoslovak champion who has helped her become the sport's hottest property.
